title: Ghost unitaries for loss-resilient photonic resource-state generation
authors: Kevin J. Randles, Manuel H. Muñoz-Arias, Kevin Thompson
abstract: Entangled few-photon states, such as Bell and Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) states, are central resources for discrete-variable photonic quantum information processing. In many architectures, these states are generated probabilistically by first heralding single photons from biphoton sources and then interfering them in linear-optical circuits. In this work, we show that the entanglement structure of said biphoton sources can be directly exploited for noise-engineering to deliver higher quality resource states. Using the transpose identity of multi-mode squeezed vacuum states, we introduce "ghost-unitary" implementations in which the target resource-generation interferometer is applied to the heralding modes rather than to the delivered resource modes. When the dominant imperfection is interferometric loss, this relocation converts direct amplitude damping of the output into false-positive heralding events that require both higher-pair emission and photon loss. In the low-squeezing regime, these events are parametrically suppressed, yielding higher-fidelity conditional resource states. We analyze this mechanism for single-qubit states, two-photon NOON states, Bell states, and a family of $n$-qubit GHZ states, as well as for single-qubit teleportation and type-I-fusion-based resource growth. Across these examples, we delineate finite parameter regimes in which ghost-unitary implementations outperform direct implementations, with particular relevance to frequency-bin photonics where active linear-optical transformations can be relatively lossy. We also prove that, in the setting considered here, the direct implementation of the $n$-GHZ family delivers identically damped outputs: equivalent to the ideal state followed by uniform amplitude damping. This extends the known $n=2,3$ cases and provides a structural result of independent interest for photonic quantum information processing.
summary: This work introduces 'ghost-unitary' methods to enhance the generation of entangled photonic resource states by engineering how the system responds to unavoidable interferometric loss. By applying the required unitary transformation to the heralding modes rather than the resource modes, the method suppresses false-positive detection events. This offers a crucial pathway for building higher-fidelity quantum computation and communication protocols using photonics.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of generating high-fidelity entangled photonic resource states (RSG) in the presence of significant interferometric loss.
main_result: The proposed 'ghost-unitary' implementation, which applies the required unitary transformation to the heralding modes instead of the resource modes, significantly improves the fidelity of generated states compared to direct methods, especially under lossy conditions.
method: The core method involves exploiting the transpose identity of multi-mode squeezed vacuum states to redefine the resource generation process, effectively reshaping the detrimental effects of amplitude damping loss.
model_or_system: The system is discrete-variable photonic quantum information processing, utilizing entangled biphoton sources (Multi-Mode Squeezed Vacuum states) to generate states like Bell, NOON, and GHZ states.
key_observables: Output fidelity ($F$), Success Probability ($p_{succ}$), and the overall Yield ($Y = p 	imes F$) for various resource states.
important_parameters: Squeezing strength ($\lambda$), various loss efficiencies ($\eta_{BS}, \eta_d, \eta_e$), and the photon number ($n$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the dominant imperfection is interferometric loss and that the ghost-unitary implementation remains well-defined despite general residual non-commuting loss.
figures_summary: Figures compare the fidelity and yield of direct versus ghost implementations for NOON states and teleportation, showing the parameter regimes where the ghost method outperforms the direct one.
paper_structure: The paper builds from background theory (MMSV states and the transpose trick) to specific analyses, comparing direct vs. ghost methods for two-photon NOON states, then extending this comparison to Bell state generation and $n$-GHZ state fidelity, and finally simulating Type-I fusion.
why_interesting: It provides a concrete, mathematically derived technique (ghost-unitary implementation) to mitigate the primary experimental hurdle in photonic quantum information—photon loss—by fundamentally changing how the loss affects the state preparation process.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. HOM-state generation in the (a) direct and (b) ghost implementations. In (a), the lossy beamsplitter acts on the delivered signal modes (top); in (b), the transposed beamsplitter acts on the heralding idler modes (bottom). For equal squeezing, both cases can be mapped onto the unified model in (c), with the implementation dependence captured by the lumped efficiencies ηs and ηi of Eq. (9).

FIG. 2. HOM-state generation comparison for equal squeezing. (a) Maximum fidelity max(F(g) HOM, F(d) HOM) and (b) fidelity difference F(g) HOM−F (d) HOM versus squeezing strength |λ|2 and beamsplitter loss rate γBS = 1 −ηBS. Here we fix ηp = 0.99 and ηd = 0.98. The solid line [white in (a), black in (b)] marks F(g) HOM = F (d) HOM; the dotted blue line in (b) is the only-beamsplitter-loss locus of Eq. (25).

FIG. 3. HOM fidelity under unequal squeezing. Main panel: Ghost implementation fidelity as a function of the squeezing parameters |λ0,1| with ηp = 0.99, ηd = 0.98, γBS = 0.1, and arg(λ0/λ1) = 0.1. Inset: corresponding direct implementation fidelity using the same scale and axes. Both plots are symmetric under λ0 ↔λ1.

FIG. 4. Heralded Bell-state generation using the (a) direct and (b) ghost implementations. The boxed interferometer in (a) is the standard four-photon, eight-mode Bell-state-generation circuit; in the ghost implementation its transpose is applied to the idler modes. The lumped efficiencies η0, · · · η3 (see legend) have implementation-dependent values; see Eq. (28). The representative click patterns ⃗σ = (1100) and ⃗ι = (00001111) are shown.

FIG. 5. Bell-state generation comparison for equal squeezing. (a) Maximum fidelity max(F(g) Bell, F(d) Bell) and (b) fidelity difference F(g) Bell −F (d) Bell versus |λ|2 and γBS. We fix ηp = 0.99, ηd = 0.98, and use a hybrid spatial- frequency model with low-loss transverse spatial beam- splitter, ηT = 0.99. The results are qualitatively similar if we take ηT = ηBS. The solid line marks F(g) Bell = F (d) Bell; the dotted blue line in (b) is the corresponding locus in the limit of only frequency-beamsplitter loss.
